snippet.title: US Reopens Russian Diesel Trade: Fuel Prices and Ukraine’s Condition | World In 30 #Shorts
snippet.description:
On October 9, 2026, US Treasury OFAC issued General License 135, temporarily authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel sales, delivery, offloading and importation, including into the United States. The exact endpoint is 12:01am US eastern daylight time on April 7, 2027. This authorization does not remove unrelated sanctions or permit debits to specified Russian state accounts at US financial institutions.

Trump describes additional supply as a way to help lower fuel prices. No completed deliveries or realized price savings are established here. Kyiv's position is attributed in the narration; no energy ceasefire is reported as agreed.

snippet.description:
Rory (W8KNX) took the California QSO Party to a Northern Michigan campground and logged 205 QSOs, including 54 of 58 California counties.
Ham2K PoLo, now with CAT control: https://polo.ham2k.com/

It's the first weekend of October, so Rory is back at the California QSO Party, this time from Wilderness State Park in Michigan, competing in the Parks on the Air overlay. He tours the camper station (FTDX10, Heil headset, a MacBook running Ham2K PoLo with CAT control), walks through putting up the Buddipole BuddiHEX solo in about 90 to 100 minutes, and shares how the weekend went: a 50/50 mix of CW and SSB, a noisy campground on 40 meters, and a near miss on a county sweep. He also wraps up with a Mackinac Bridge vs Golden Gate Bridge comparison.

snippet.title: What Happened to the D-104? Astatic Never Owned the Crystal
snippet.description:
Astatic built the D-104 in Youngstown, Ohio, at 830 Market Street, and later in Conneaut on the shore of Lake Erie. The first ad ran in QST in November 1933, list price $17.50. The crystal version stayed in production for 68 years.

You squeezed the bar and the relays slammed over behind you. Round chrome head, wire mesh, the slide switch and the nine-volt battery in the amplified T-UG8 stand. The response rose to a peak near 3,000 cycles, and the reports came back that your audio was cutting right through the pileup. On CB it was the Silver Eagle.

The crystal was never Astatic's. The Rochelle salt was made under Brush patents, and Brush licensed the same technology to Shure. Once ceramic arrived, anyone could build a hot microphone. Astatic owned a shape and a sound. The crystal D-104 ended in 2001; on September 1, 2009, the Astatic name was folded into CAD Audio.

73.

snippet.title: Qualified But Stuck: The Aircraft Licence Catch 22 Facing Young Technicians | Adrian Otieno
snippet.description:
Trained. Qualified. Still locked out of the hangar. Avionics technician Adrian Otieno explains the aviation licence catch-22 facing young aircraft maintenance graduates in Kenya and across Africa.

You finish your aviation training. To get hired, you need a licence from the regulator. To get the licence, you need logged, signed-off experience on real aircraft. And that experience only comes with the job.

In this episode of African Aviation Conversations, we sit down with Adrian Otieno, a young avionics technician in Nairobi, to talk about what happens after graduation, and why so many trained technicians struggle to take the next step.

The demand is real. ICAO estimates the industry will need to recruit around 665,000 aircraft maintenance technicians worldwide by 2037. In Kenya, an avionics (B2) aircraft maintenance engineer licence requires at least two years of practical maintenance experience, even after completing an approved training course. The talent exists and the demand exists. What is missing is the bridge between the two.

IN THIS CONVERSATION

snippet.title: The Solar Adapter Every Go Bag Needs
snippet.description:
Can you plug a solar panel straight into your phone, power bank, or handheld ham radio without a power station or charge controller in between? In this video I put the Diffpower 65W Solar Converter to the test and find out if this simple PV to USB-C adapter actually delivers in the real world.
The Diffpower solar converter takes the MC4 output from a standard solar panel and turns it into USB-C Power Delivery (PD 3.0) output. That means you can connect a portable solar panel directly to your USB-C devices and charge them using nothing but sunlight. No battery bank in the middle, no charge controller, and no complicated wiring.
I tested it three ways. First, I used it to recharge a USB-C battery bank so I could store solar energy for later. Next, I charged a cell phone directly from the solar panel. Finally, I charged a handheld ham radio over USB-C, which is a big deal for anyone building an off grid or emergency communications kit.
If you are into EmComm, ARES, POTA, SOTA, camping, overlanding, backpacking, or emergency preparedness, a small solar to USB-C adapter like this can simplify your power setup and lighten your go bag. More and more gear charges over USB-C these days, including many modern handheld radios, so being able to feed that gear straight from a solar panel opens up a lot of options when the grid is down or you are far from an outlet.
I also talk about what to expect when charging directly from solar, how weather and panel size affect performance, and where this adapter fits compared to carrying a full portable power station.
Have you tried charging your radio or phone directly from a solar panel? Let me know in the comments what setup you use for off grid USB-C charging.

But the other part of it is hopefully illustrated in this video.  You get to explore.  You get to go places you otherwise wouldn't, or couldn't.  You get to see new locations.  Scout potential future activation sites.  Find a little place in the forest to call your own.  Away from noise, away from people.  Beautiful scenery and abundant fresh air.  Just you, nature, and your radio.

snippet.title: They Turned an Empty Spacesuit Into a Satellite 👨‍🚀
snippet.description:
In 2006, the crew of the International Space Station deliberately pushed a retired Russian Orlan spacesuit into orbit. But this wasn't simply space junk. The suit had been repurposed into SuitSat-1, an experimental amateur-radio satellite.
Inside the suit were batteries, temperature sensors, a radio transmitter, and a CD containing messages and images from students around the world. As it orbited Earth, amateur radio operators could tune in and receive recorded greetings, telemetry about the suit, and other signals.
The experiment was designed to turn an old spacesuit into something useful for education and amateur radio. The radio signal ended much sooner than expected, after only a few days, and SuitSat-1 eventually reentered Earth's atmosphere and burned up.

snippet.title: U.S. Eases Sanctions on Russian Diesel
snippet.description:
The U.S. Treasury on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026 issued Russia-related General License 135, authorizing the sale, delivery, offloading and importation, including into the United States, of Russian-origin diesel through 12:01 a.m. EDT on April 7, 2027. President Trump said, after a call with Vladimir Putin, that Russia will immediately release more than 300,000 tons of diesel, with more promised later; Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told TASS that Russia is lifting its diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule.

The administration says added supply will help bring diesel prices down. U.S. average retail diesel was $6.20 a gallon in the week of Oct. 5, up about 63% from $3.81 in late February, after a record $6.53 in the week of Sept. 21 (EIA). Diesel futures fell about 4% Friday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called easing sanctions without a lasting de-escalation agreement "an obvious weakness" that lets Russia "wage war for longer." The move came as Ukrainian negotiators met U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami for peace talks.

Information as of about 3:40 p.m. MST, Oct. 9, 2026.

Sources:
- U.S. Treasury OFAC, General License 135: https://ofac.treasury.gov/recent-actions/20261009_33 (PDF: https://ofac.treasury.gov/media/937216/download?inline=)
- U.S. Energy Information Administration, weekly U.S. No. 2 diesel retail prices: https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=EMD_EPD2D_PTE_NUS_DPG&f=W

snippet.title: Top 10 Tools Every Beginning DXer Needs | NA9P at W9DXCC
snippet.description:
Jeff Bolling NA9P delivered one of the most interesting presentations I heard at this year's W9DXCC convention: Top 10 Tools the Beginning DXer Shouldn't Be Without.

We're doing something a little different on Q5 this week. Jeff joins me to reprise his W9DXCC presentation in its entirety, followed by questions and discussion about his remarkable progress as a relatively new amateur radio operator.

Licensed in October 2024, Jeff has already confirmed 178 DX entities, operating with just 100 watts and a wire antenna from a suburban Illinois lot. His presentation draws on that experience, offering ten practical tools and strategies for getting more DX in the log, including propagation planning, GridTracker, contesting, CW, Club Log, and QSL management.

What makes Jeff's perspective particularly interesting is that he's learning DXing in today's amateur radio environment, with today's technology and the guidance of experienced operators from the Northern Illinois DX Association. His presentation is valuable not only for beginning DXers, but also for experienced operators interested in mentoring the next generation.

Join the conversation and subscribe to Q5 Worldwide Ham Radio.

snippet.title: 6 Million Barrels of Russian Diesel: What the US Just Allowed #shorts#diesel
snippet.description:
On October 9, 2026, President Trump said Russia agreed to immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, another 500,000 tons in November, and 1,000,000 tons right after that. The same day, the Treasury Department issued a temporary general license allowing Russian diesel into the global market, which Reuters reports runs through April 7. The Kremlin said Russia is ready to supply oil and oil products; the specific volumes came from Trump. 

The first two shipments total about 6 million barrels, roughly a day and a half of US diesel demand, according to the Energy Information Administration as cited by CNN. Analysts said the amount is unlikely to move prices much, reporting notes Russian refineries have been damaged by Ukrainian attacks, and Ukraine’s president condemned the deal. Parts of the Russia sanctions law signed September 18 also come due on October 19. Here’s what was announced, what was licensed, and what’s still unconfirmed, with no spin.

snippet.title: One Radio Modem to Rule Them ALL!
snippet.description:
Let's run Modem73 on two Pi's and communicate over Ham radio using TCP/IP, AX.25 and Web.  Modem73 is among the new open-source modems implementing "OFDM" encodings getting us (relatively) high speed networking with packet radio.   Modem 73 supports OFDM/Robust/MFSK, which, in this case was transmitting QAM16 at 3.6Kb/s using off-the-shelf radios - TIDRadio H9 and Yaesu FTM400.  Modem73 supports both HF and VHF, so we could possibly see this as an alternative VARAHF for Winlink Email on HF and local AX25/IP networks on VHF.

Modem73 is supported on MacOS, Windows, Linux and Android.

https://modem73.app/
https://modem73.app/quickstart.html
https://github.com/RFnexus/modem73

snippet.title: CW POTA with a 1966 Vibroplex Bug! | US-2991 Bonham State Park
snippet.description:
This POTA activation at US-2991 Bonham State Park in Texas was a little different — I brought out a 1966 Vibroplex Champion bug to celebrate Bugout October!
Operating from the park, I used the Vibroplex bug for the first half of the activation. It was a lot of fun sending with this classic piece of Morse code history, and I can only hope the POTA hunters had as much fun copying my fist as I had sending it!

For the second half of the activation, NZ5K Mike Mitchell joins me for some more CW and conversation from the park.
As always, this is filmed from the operator's point of view, putting you right at the operating position so you can follow along and practice copying the Morse code just as if you were there with me.

Station & Equipment
• Yaesu FT-891
• LDG Z-100 Plus ATU
• 20 Ah Bioenno LiFePO4 battery
• 1966 Vibroplex Champion bug
• 29-foot End-Fed Random Wire (EFRW)
• Homebrew 9:1 unun
• 7-meter Spiderbeam mast

📍 POTA US-2991 — Bonham State Park, Texas

If you enjoy Parks on the Air, QRP, CW, Morse code, portable amateur radio, straight keys and bugs, this activation is for you.
Thanks to all the hunters who put in the effort to copy the bug — and a special thanks to Mike Mitchell, NZ5K, for joining me for the second half of the activation.

snippet.title: Xiegu G7250: ONE Number That Could Change Which Ham Radio You Buy
snippet.description:
What does your money actually buy when you choose an amateur radio?

The new Xiegu G7250 got me thinking. Instead of another specifications comparison, what if we borrowed a trick from finance and reduced these very different HF transceivers to ONE deliberately simple number?

$/dBm: the purchase price divided by the maximum RF output expressed in dBm.

It gives us a fascinating starting point:

QRP Labs QMX+ — $5.41/dBm
Xiegu G7250 — $19.98/dBm
Icom IC-7300MK2 — $28.00/dBm
Yaesu FTX-1 Optima — $39.00/dBm
FlexRadio FLEX-8400 + ATU + Maestro — $88.96/dBm

And, of course, that does NOT tell us which is the ‘best’ radio.

That is precisely the point.

A radio is far more than watts and purchase price. The Yaesu FTX-1 Optima adds VHF and UHF. The FlexRadio system offers a very different networked SDR architecture and operating environment. The Icom IC-7300MK2 brings Icom’s engineering, ecosystem and dealer support. The remarkable little QMX+ gives us 5 W rather than 100 W. And the new Xiegu G7250 combines 100 W HF, 6 m, a direct-sampling SDR, internal ATU and a separate 7-inch control head for $999.

So $/dBm isn’t a verdict. It is a heuristic.

It gives us a common financial starting line and then forces the question that really matters:

WHAT AM I GETTING FOR THE EXTRA MONEY?

Receiver performance? Transmit signal quality? Additional bands? SDR capability? Ergonomics? Firmware? Build quality? Support? Reliability? Resale value? Portability? Remote operation?

Instead of beginning with the badge on the front, perhaps we should start with what we actually need a radio to do, establish what its RF output costs us, and then decide which additional capabilities are genuinely worth paying for.

In this video I compare the new Xiegu G7250 with the QRP Labs QMX+, Icom IC-7300MK2, Yaesu FTX-1 Optima and a FLEX-8400 system with ATU and Maestro.

One number cannot tell you which radio to buy.

But it might make you ask much better questions before you do.

73,
Dave, G3LRC
